items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules whatsoever
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher's four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue 'love' as sole criterion is too vague; defenders argue agape has specific New Testament content that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.

items.title: The Khalsa was founded at Vaisakhi 1699
items.claim: What did Guru Gobind Singh establish in 1699?

options.text: A new Sikh state in northern India

The Khalsa ('the pure') — a community of initiated Sikhs marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan), open to all castes and genders, with surnames Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women
A revised version of the Guru Granth Sahib
A peace treaty with the Mughal Empire

items.reveal:
At Anandpur on Vaisakhi (April) 1699, Guru Gobind Singh called for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) came forward, were initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword), and were then themselves used to initiate Gobind Singh.

The Five Ks: Kesh (uncut hair, including the dastaar turban), Kara (steel bracelet), Kanga (wooden comb), Kachera (cotton undergarment), Kirpan (small sword).

The Khalsa took the surnames Singh and Kaur, symbolically equalising caste and gender.
items.why: Sikh identity has visible bodily markers from a specific 1699 event with named participants. The Five Ks are not vague cultural symbols but coded responses to Mughal-era persecution and caste hierarchy.

items.title: Paley's watchmaker argument was published in 1802

options.text: If we found a stone on a heath, we would infer no designer
If we found a watch on a heath, the complexity and purposive arrangement of its parts would compel us to infer a watchmaker — and similar reasoning applied to nature implies a divine designer
Nature is too random to need a designer
The argument compares the universe to a clockwork mechanism explicitly

items.reveal:
William Paley's 'Natural Theology' (1802) opens with the watch-on-the-heath analogy. He uses the human eye as his prime biological example.

Hume's 'Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion' (1779, published posthumously) anticipated and refuted versions of the design argument decades earlier — the analogy is weak (the universe is not like a watch), there are flaws (suggesting an apprentice designer or a committee), and the argument cannot reach a single benevolent God.

Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) provided a non-design explanation for biological complexity. Modern Intelligent Design (Behe, Dembski, 1990s onwards) is a controversial attempt to revive the argument scientifically.
items.why: The design argument keeps returning in new forms. Each version has to deal with the next development in science — biological evolution, cosmic fine-tuning, multiverse cosmology — making it a moving target rather than a settled debate.
